clue.text: Beastly utterance about public house shows pizzazz

indicators.note: 'about' can mean turned around, as in an about-turn, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: the sound a cow makes
PH is the map abbreviation for a public house

explanation.surface: An animal's noise heard around the pub is praised as showing real flair.
explanation.walkthrough: A public house is a pub; PH marks one on British maps.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are informal nouns for energetic vitality, liveliness and attractive flair.

clue.text: Where to see Isaac and Ruth regularly collude with Will

definitions.text: Where to see Isaac and Ruth

indicators.note: something done regularly happens at even intervals, so every other letter is taken

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters
a will is a last testament

explanation.surface: Two people called Isaac and Ruth keep conspiring with a third friend called Will.
explanation.walkthrough: Isaac and Ruth look like fodder to be mined for letters, but they belong to the definition; the letters come from 'collude'. 'Will' loses its capital and means a legal document.
explanation.definitionFit: Isaac and Ruth are figures from the Hebrew scriptures, the first part of the Christian Bible, whose books tell their stories.

clue.text: Day before fast run, tucking into bananas, I cut grass

indicators.note: cutting something shortens it, so the final letter is dropped
to tuck into a thing is to slip inside it, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: bananas is slang for crazy
R is the cricket abbreviation for a run
taken as written
grass with its last letter removed

explanation.surface: Someone mowing a lawn on the eve of a fast, while running around eating bananas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bananas' looks like fruit but means crazy. The definition is the whole phrase 'Day before fast', with fast meaning Lent.
explanation.definitionFit: This carnival is Shrove Tuesday, the day of feasting before the Lenten fast begins on Ash Wednesday.

clue.text: That man Trump, oddly angry

parts.note: the pronoun for a man

indicators.note: 'oddly' points to the odd-numbered positions, first, third and fifth

parts.note: the first, third and fifth letters

explanation.surface: A jibe at a politician who is strangely furious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oddly' reads as 'strangely' in the surface, but it picks the odd letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The informal British phrase describes someone agitated, worked up and upset, a close match for furious.

clue.text: Stood by US ex-president, one making bloomers

parts.note: rose is the past tense of rise, to stand up
either George Bush, a former American president

explanation.surface: Someone stood beside a former American president, perhaps one who commits gaffes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloomers' suggests blunders or baggy underwear; here it means things that bloom, flowers.
explanation.definitionFit: The plant produces blooms, so it is literally a maker of flowers, a playful sense of the word for gaffes.

clue.text: Neckwear fit for a king generates cash for writers

parts.note: regal, suitable for a monarch
ties are worn round the neck

explanation.surface: Designer neckties good enough for a monarch earn their makers money.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue gives the neckwear first, but it is read as regal ties, so the adjective goes in front.
explanation.definitionFit: Authors receive payments per copy sold of their books, a share of the earnings from publishers.

clue.text: Average appeal for help and love

parts.note: the Morse distress signal
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O

explanation.surface: Ordinary cries for rescue and for affection.
explanation.walkthrough: Love means nil in tennis scoring, hence the letter O.
explanation.definitionFit: Both describe something mediocre, neither particularly good nor bad, merely middling.

clue.text: 80s singer's expression of astonishment, bagging Oscar

indicators.note: to bag something is to put it inside a bag, so one piece is enclosed

parts.note: the old exclamation of surprise 'By George!'
Oscar is O in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A pop star gasps with amazement on winning an Academy Award.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oscar' suggests the film award; it is simply the radio code word for O.
explanation.definitionFit: The frontman of Culture Club was a famous pop star of the 1980s, known for his flamboyant style.

clue.text: Say nothing revolutionary, or just a little bit

parts.note: the call for silence
a red is a communist revolutionary

explanation.surface: Advice to a radical: keep quiet, or at most say very little.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue the two pieces stack in order; RED for a revolutionary is a standard convention.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun names a tiny scrap or fragment, as in 'not a shred of evidence'.

clue.text: Female novelist and Harry Styles do badly, receiving nothing

indicators.note: to receive something is to take it in, so another letter goes inside
doing something badly leaves it in a mess, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: the letters of the pop star's name plus 'do'
nothing is zero, shaped like O

explanation.surface: A woman writer and the pop star Harry Styles both flop, earning nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'do' belongs to the fodder rather than the surface verb it seems to be; the added O makes up the letter count.
explanation.definitionFit: She was an English writer of detective fiction, creator of the sleuth Lord Peter Wimsey.

clue.text: Reworked Monet or Paris impressionist

indicators.note: reworked material has been redone in a new form, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An Impressionist painter's work, perhaps a Monet or a Paris scene, is revised.
explanation.walkthrough: Monet and Paris make 'impressionist' look like the art movement; it means a mimic.
explanation.definitionFit: An impressionist in entertainment mimics famous people, which is exactly what a comic mimic does.

clue.text: Former pilot organised large, election-day survey

parts.note: ex means former

indicators.note: organising things puts them into a new order, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: An ex-pilot runs a big poll on voting day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Former pilot' reads as one person, but EX and the anagram fodder are separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Pollsters question voters as they leave the polling station, giving an early forecast of results.

clue.text: Model's working on rare occasions

indicators.note: working material is being processed and reshaped, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters of the word with its S

explanation.surface: A fashion model only gets work now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe S reads as 'is' but its S joins the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb means infrequently, hardly ever, matching the phrase exactly.

clue.text: Bully, caught in daft error, is embarrassed

indicators.note: something caught in a net sits within it, so the letters lie inside the following words

parts.note: running across the words, from the end of the first to the start of the last

explanation.surface: A bully who makes a silly mistake is red-faced.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer spans dafT ERROR IS Embarrassed, ignoring the comma.
explanation.definitionFit: As verbs, both mean to intimidate someone with threats and fear.

clue.text: Stink raised by domestic worker having sharp eyes

indicators.note: in a down clue, raising a word makes it read upwards, from bottom to top

parts.note: BO is body odour
a household servant

explanation.surface: A smell is kicked up by a sharp-eyed housemaid.
explanation.walkthrough: BO, short for body odour, is a common abbreviation for a stink.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone quick to notice details is described as perceptive and watchful, with keen sight.

clue.text: Article I stuffed into leotard I designed

indicators.note: stuffing something into a thing packs it inside
a design gives things a new arrangement, so these letters are reshaped

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A dancer boasts of a feature about the leotard they designed and filled.
explanation.walkthrough: The first I is added to the second group, then all nine letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A newspaper's leading article giving the paper's own opinion is its leader column.

clue.text: Scoundrel's regret, letting own goal in

indicators.note: letting something in admits it inside, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: to rue is to regret
the football abbreviation

explanation.surface: A villainous defender is sorry for conceding an own goal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'letting ... in' wraps round the own goal; OG is the standard football abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Both nouns name a dishonest, unprincipled rascal or villain.

clue.text: What martial artist might wear in unspoilt area

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a coloured grade sash in judo or karate
second meaning: protected countryside round a town

explanation.surface: A judo fighter training out in the countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain, protected rural land around cities where building is restricted has this name.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is both an intermediate rank marker in karate and a planning term for preserved countryside.

clue.text: British supermodel smuggles ecstasy for prophet

indicators.note: smuggled goods are hidden inside something, so one piece is concealed within another

parts.note: Kate Moss, the British model
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: A famous model is caught smuggling drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: Kate Moss is a well-known British supermodel; E is slang for an ecstasy pill.
explanation.definitionFit: The biblical leader who received the Ten Commandments is regarded as a great prophet.

clue.text: Cowardly son unfortunately sleeps in

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for son

indicators.note: an unfortunate outcome is a mishap, so these letters go awry into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A lazy, gutless son is lying in bed again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' looks like part of the phrase 'sleeps in' and it is, but as fodder rather than meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacking a backbone is the idiom for lacking courage, so the word means timid and weak-willed.

clue.text: Flowers, trees etc. aren't cultivated round university

indicators.note: to go round something is to surround it
cultivated land is worked over and turned, so these letters are reworked

parts.note: the letters without the apostrophe
U is the abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: Plants growing wild around a campus are not tended.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cultivated' seems to belong with flowers and trees, but it works on the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: The natural world of plants and wildlife is collectively called by this word; 'etc.' shows the definition is by example.

clue.text: Time on top of mature bull

indicators.note: in a down clue, sitting on top means coming first in the column

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for time
fully developed

explanation.surface: Time spent on the back of a full-grown bull.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bull' looks like the animal but is short for nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are slang nouns for rubbish or nonsense talk.

clue.text: Understand conservative von Bismarck gets refusal from France

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for Conservative
Otto von Bismarck, the German chancellor
French for no

explanation.surface: A right-wing German statesman is turned down by the French.
explanation.walkthrough: Bismarck's first name was Otto, so 'von Bismarck' stands for it.
explanation.definitionFit: The informal phrasal verb means to grasp or realise something, to catch on.

clue.text: Coach heads for the undulating hill

indicators.note: the head of a word is its beginning, so first letters are taken

parts.note: the first letters of these two words
a tor is a rocky hill

explanation.surface: A bus trip sets off towards rolling hills.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coach' reads as a bus heading somewhere; it means a teacher. A tor is a rocky hilltop, as on Dartmoor.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are nouns for a private teacher who instructs or trains a pupil.

clue.text: Iberian country saving one bridge

indicators.note: 'saving' can mean except, so one letter is left out

parts.note: the country on the Iberian peninsula
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A country in Iberia rescues one of its bridges.
explanation.walkthrough: 'saving' looks like rescuing but means 'except', as in 'all saving one'.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb, to cross over a gap or river is to straddle it, as a bridge does.

clue.text: Diana's engagement is a let-down

parts.note: Di is short for Diana, with the possessive S
a scheduled meeting

explanation.surface: Princess Diana's marriage engagement proved to be a letdown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'engagement' suggests betrothal, but it is a booked meeting.
explanation.definitionFit: Both nouns describe something that fails to live up to hopes or expectations.

clue.text: Guard, to some extent, present in Elsinore

indicators.note: only partly, so just a portion of the following words is used

parts.note: running from inside the first word to the start of the last

explanation.surface: A guard is posted at Elsinore, Hamlet's castle.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run through preSENT IN ELsinore. Hamlet opens with sentries on the battlements of Elsinore.
explanation.definitionFit: Both nouns name a soldier or watchman posted to keep watch.

clue.text: Turning mechanism going in either direction?

indicators.note: a word that reads the same whichever way it goes is the same forwards and backwards

parts.note: a rotating part of a machine

explanation.surface: A spinning part that can turn clockwise or anticlockwise.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that 'either direction' means reading the word, not spinning the part.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the rotating component of a motor, helicopter or engine.
